text: A reference field is a field on one table that points to a specific record on another table — ServiceNow's version of a foreign key. The clearest example: incident has a caller_id field that references a record on sys_user, the person who reported the incident. Relationally, this is exactly a foreign key — one table's field holds a pointer to a row in another table, rather than duplicating that row's data inline.

Here's the detail that trips up new admins. A reference field like caller_id displays the caller's name, say Fred Luddy, but what it actually stores is that sys_user record's sys_id. The name you see on the form is a live lookup against the referenced record's display value, not text sitting in the caller_id column itself. If that user's name is ever changed in sys_user, every incident referencing them updates its displayed name automatically.

Because a reference field has to resolve to one specific record on a potentially huge table, ServiceNow gives it a distinct interface. Start typing into caller_id and an auto-complete list filters live, matching against the referenced table's display field. Once a value is set, a small info icon appears next to the field — clicking it opens a preview of that referenced record's email, phone, and department, without navigating away from the form you're already on.

A related list shows the reverse direction of that same relationship. Open a sys_user record for a specific person, and a related list below the form can show every incident where that user is the caller_id. The platform is simply running the equivalent of find every incident whose caller_id equals this user's sys_id, and rendering the results inline. Chapter 5 covers related lists in real depth — for now, recognize they're two views of one relationship.

Once you can recognize a reference field, you can read any unfamiliar table's structure and immediately know which other tables it connects to, and in which direction. An incident record connects outward to sys_user, through caller_id and assigned_to, and to sys_user_group through assignment_group — three separate pointers, visible the moment you know to look for reference-type fields. Next up: a worked lab tying every idea from this chapter together.
